The project started on 1 March with all 14 facilities assessed in the first weeks and the first cohort of health workers trained. Mentors reached facilities from the second week, community health volunteers were already running dialogue sessions, and first antenatal visits and immunization numbers began to rise. Field report, March 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: all 14 facilities were visited with the health care waste checklist. Sharps containers and safety boxes were in place in 12 of 14 facilities; two dispensaries (Nakwamekwi and Napuu) received replacement sharps boxes and a placenta pit was dug at Napuu. Segregated waste bins were distributed to the maternity wings during the visits. No environmental incidents were reported. Branding and marking: the USAID identity was applied to training banners, the CHV training kits and the sign-in sheets used in March; no equipment was delivered in March so no equipment marking was needed. Coordination: the team attended the Turkana County health sector coordination meeting and the sub-county cold chain meeting, and briefed the County Director of Health on the start-up plan. Gender: two female nurse mentors were recruited among the five mentors, and training schedules were set to finish before 3 pm so that women health workers could travel home in daylight.

Recruitment of the nurse mentors and the first procurement round took longer than planned, so services were only partly covered in the first weeks. USAID rules required three quotations for each equipment lot, which delayed the first delivery.
Most indicators are below their monthly share of the target because March was a start-up month: training, equipment and community structures were still being put in place.
Mentors were deployed in the second week instead of the first, and the training calendar was compressed so the missed days were recovered in April.
Pairing a classroom course with an on-site mentorship visit within two weeks lets health workers apply the new skills straight away.

Both trainings and mentorship ran at full pace, and the first equipment kits reached three facilities. Immunization and antenatal numbers rose well above March. Field report, April 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: waste management follow-up visits were made to all 14 facilities; sharps boxes were collected and incinerated at Lodwar Sub-County Hospital by the county incinerator team, and placenta pits were checked at the six facilities that conduct deliveries. The flooding washed out one placenta pit at Kalokol, which was rebuilt on higher ground. No other incidents. Branding and marking: USAID marking was applied to the first three equipment kits and to the solar refrigerators delivered; the marking plan approved by the AOR was followed. Coordination: the team attended the County health sector coordination meeting, the nutrition technical working group and the cold chain meeting; flood updates were shared with the county disaster management committee. Gender: transport vouchers were prioritised for women with danger signs during the road closures, and women CHVs formed the majority of the second CHV cohort.
Long-rains flooding on the Turkwel and Kerio rivers cut the Kalokol and Lowarengak roads for nine days, so two outreach sites could not be visited. A national Penta vaccine shortage lasted one week.
Some counts, such as skilled deliveries, are still behind their planned monthly share because roads were cut during the rains and two outreach sites were missed.
Outreach routes were re-planned around the flooded roads, and children missed during the stock-out were recalled for vaccination in the following weeks.
A fixed outreach calendar shared with community health volunteers helps caregivers find outreach sessions even when routes change.

Antenatal attendance and skilled deliveries kept rising and the transport voucher scheme was used by more women than before. Penta3 coverage passed 70 percent at supported facilities and a community KAP spot survey was completed. Field report, May 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: waste management checks continued at all 14 facilities; the incinerator team collected and burned sharps waste at Lodwar Sub-County Hospital and Lokichar Health Centre during the nurses' strike so that waste did not accumulate. No incidents. Branding and marking: all four equipment kits delivered in May carried USAID marking and the handover certificates recorded it; radio scripts for the community messages acknowledged USAID. Coordination: weekly calls with the sub-county health management team were held during the strike; the project agreed mobile clinic schedules with the County Director of Health. Gender: mobile antenatal clinics were staffed by women clinical officers where possible, and the KAP survey enumerators were balanced by sex.
A county nurses' industrial action lasted twelve days and reduced clinic hours at five facilities.

Results held up despite the strike because project-supported clinical officers ran mobile clinics; community dialogue days were the largest so far, which pushed the number of people reached above plan.
Mobile antenatal and immunization clinics were run at the affected facilities for the duration of the strike.
Having project clinical officers able to cover for striking colleagues kept services open without replacing the county's own staff.

Equipment kits reached four more facilities, taking the total to eleven, and skilled delivery rose to more than half of deliveries at supported facilities. KHIS reporting became timelier. Field report, June 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: waste management checks were completed at all 14 facilities; two solar refrigerators that failed were repaired and the failed batteries were returned to the supplier for recycling rather than discarded. No incidents. Branding and marking: USAID marking was applied to the repaired refrigerators and to the four new kits delivered in June; one health worker training banner was replaced after weather damage. Coordination: the team briefed the Sub-County Commander on the security situation near Lorugum and agreed an escort for outreach; the county cold chain officer joined the repair planning. Gender: women attendants accompanied the outreach teams for deliveries and family planning counselling, and the maternal death notification was reported through the MPDSR channel with no identifying details recorded.
Solar refrigerators failed at two facilities and cattle-raid insecurity near Lorugum suspended outreach there for a week.
Immunization numbers dipped slightly against plan because of the cold-chain failures and the suspended outreach; mentorship visits and community education remained on plan.
Vaccines were temporarily moved to the nearest working cold chain, the two refrigerators were repaired within eight days, and outreach resumed with an escort arranged by the sub-county commander.
A weekly cold-chain temperature check shared by phone with the sub-county cold-chain officer catches failures before vaccines are lost.

Training reached its target pace, nearly all facilities were equipped and ANC4+ coverage rose to 43 percent. Community volunteers screened a record number of children for malnutrition. Field report, July 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: waste management checks continued at all 14 facilities; the CMAM sites received segregated bins for RUTF packaging and the county collected the packaging. No incidents. Branding and marking: USAID marking was applied to the MUAC tapes and referral slips printed in July and to the two final equipment kits. Coordination: the project took part in the county nutrition cluster response to the drought, and the county health management team asked the CHVs' screening data to be shared in the weekly drought bulletin. Gender: screening days at water points were timed to avoid the hours women collect water, and mothers with infants were seen first.
Drought deepened across Turkana South and malnutrition screening numbers rose sharply; some caregivers walked long distances to reach screening points.
The number of children screened and referred is higher than planned because drought drove more caregivers to seek care, so screening and referral are above the target pace.
CHV screening days were moved to water points and market days, and referral transport for severe cases was organised with the county.
Screening at water points finds more children than house-to-house visits during drought.

The final month closed training, equipment and CHV activity. All 14 facilities are equipped, 220 CHVs are trained and the final KAP survey shows a large rise in caregiver knowledge of danger signs. Coverage targets for ANC4+, skilled delivery and Penta3 were met or nearly met. Field report, August 2026 (LOCHA programme team). Environmental compliance under the IEE: the final waste management audit covered all 14 facilities; all sharps containers were in place and the placenta pits were in good condition; the project's waste management checklist was handed to the sub-county public health officers. No incidents during the activity. Branding and marking: a final marking audit of equipment, the 14 solar and kit installations and training materials found all items marked; the audit sheet is held with the handover certificates. Coordination: the final handover meeting was held with the County Executive Committee Member for Health, the Director of Health, the sub-county health management teams and the USAID AOR. Gender: women made up most CHVs and most people reached with health education; the handover tools include the sex-disaggregated registers.
Handover of solar fridges and registers to the county needed more signatures than expected, and the final KAP survey fell in a week of hot weather with low turnout in two villages.

Some count targets were slightly missed, for example immunization and first antenatal visits, because of the floods, the nurses' strike and the cold-chain failures earlier in the project; coverage rates reached or exceeded their targets.
The sub-county health management team signed the asset handover certificates and the two villages were revisited for the KAP survey.
Handing tools and registers to the county in the final month is smoother when the sub-county team has been joining the monthly data review since the start.
